# QHome 2.1.0 help

This file has the same pages as the **Help** tab of QHome. In the app the pages show your own address and names; here they are examples: the page is at `http://192.168.1.50:7000`, the master's address is `192.168.1.50`, the node name is `qhome`, the MQTT port is 1883 and the USB helper port is 7001.

## Contents

- [Getting started](#start)
- [Pins and devices](#pins)
- [Connecting boards](#wiring)
- [Board models](#boards)
- [Blocks cookbook](#blocks)
- [LED matrix](#matrix)
- [MQTT and Home Assistant](#mqtt)
- [Troubleshooting](#faq)

<a id="start"></a>
## Getting started

QHome turns the Arduino UNO Q into a smart-home controller without writing code. One general firmware is uploaded once. After that every pin gets its job in this web page, and **Save & apply** makes a change live at once. Nothing is compiled or uploaded again.

You are looking at QHome 2.1.0 at **http://192.168.1.50:7000**.

<a id="start-install"></a>
### Install on the UNO Q

1. Copy the `qhome` folder to `~/ArduinoApps/qhome` on the board: with App Lab's import, with `scp`, or with the VS Code task **UNO Q: deploy the app**.
2. In App Lab open the app, go to **Sketch Libraries** and add **Arduino_RouterBridge**.
3. Press **Run**. The first start compiles the sketch and uploads it to the microcontroller.
4. App Lab opens this page in your browser as soon as QHome answers.

If no page opens, the address is shown in these places:

- **Python console** of App Lab: a framed block with `http://<address>:7000`. The same lines are in the **Log** tab.
- **Serial Monitor** of App Lab: `=== QHome ===` and the address. It is printed every 30 seconds, so after you open the monitor it can take up to half a minute to appear; from then on press any key in the monitor to see it at once.
- **LED matrix**: with **Show** set to **Web address** it scrolls the address. See [LED matrix](#matrix-modes).
- Or type `http://<board-name>.local:7000`, with the name the UNO Q was given when it was set up.

> **Note:** With a web password set, App Lab cannot open the page by itself. Open the address by hand. See [Troubleshooting](#faq-password).

<a id="start-tabs"></a>
### The six tabs

| Tab | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard | Starts with the **System** panel: board name, clock and time zone, uptime, CPU, memory, storage, temperature, the web address and versions. Below it one tile per device, with live values and switches. |
| Boards & pins | Add boards and give each pin a job. |
| Blocks | Automations, built from Scratch-style blocks. |
| Settings | Name, time zone, web password, role, MQTT and Home Assistant, backup. |
| Log | What QHome did and what went wrong. |
| Help | These pages. |

A UNO Q in the node role has four of them: Dashboard, Settings, Log and Help.

<a id="start-first-device"></a>
### Your first device

1. Open **Boards & pins**. The board is drawn as it looks, with the USB connector on the left.
2. Click a free pin. Its coloured marks show what it can do.
3. Pick a job from the list and give the device a name.
4. Press **Save & apply**. The device appears on the **Dashboard**.

The jobs a pin can get:

| Tag | Device | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DI | Button or contact | Push button, door contact, PIR, limit switch |
| AI | Analog sensor | Potentiometer, NTC, LDR, any voltage sensor |
| CNT | Pulse counter | Flow meter, energy meter, RPM |
| DO | Relay or LED | Anything that is simply on or off |
| PWM | Dimmer (PWM) | LED brightness, fan or motor speed |
| AO | Analog output | A real voltage from the DAC |
| RGB | RGB LED | On-board LED, 8 colours |
| MX | LED matrix | Text, clock, live values, graphs, icons, animations |
| VS | Virtual switch | A flag for scripts and Home Assistant |

Details for each kind are in [Pins and devices](#pins).

<a id="start-first-script"></a>
### Your first script

1. Open **Blocks** and drag `when ... turns on` out of **Events**. Choose your button in it.
2. Snap `toggle ...` from **Devices** under it and choose your relay.
3. Press **Save & apply**. The script runs from that moment.

More examples are in the [Blocks cookbook](#blocks-recipes).

<a id="start-simulator"></a>
### Try it without hardware

On a PC, start QHome with a simulated UNO Q:

```
QHOME_MODE=sim python python/main.py
```

- The browser opens `http://localhost:7000` by itself. Set `QHOME_OPEN_BROWSER=0` to stop that.
- A **Simulation** badge shows at the top. Analog inputs wander, and every simulated input has a **Hold to press (simulation)** button on the Dashboard.
- Boards you add are simulated too, so every board model can be tried.
- To see how a found board is announced, start with `QHOME_SIM_DISCOVER=esp32@wifi:porch`.

<a id="start-where"></a>
### What runs where

- Scripts run on the Linux side of the master. They stop while the master is off.
- Other boards keep their outputs as they were while the master is away.
- When QHome starts, each output does what its **After a restart** setting says.

<a id="pins"></a>
## Pins and devices

**Boards & pins** draws each board with its pins where they are on the real board, USB connector on the left. **List view** shows the same pins as plain rows.

- A free pin carries coloured marks for what it can do. Click it and pick a job.
- A hatched pin is used by a board link (for example D0 and D1 for UART) and cannot get a job.
- An amber corner marks a boot pin or an input-only pin. Read its notes before you wire anything to it.
- Grey pads (GND, 5V, 3V3, RST and so on) are shown for orientation and cannot be configured.

What each board offers:

| Board | Logic | Digital pins | PWM | Analog in | Analog out | Counter | Also on the board |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Arduino UNO Q | 3.3 V | 25 | 13 | 6 (14 bit) | 2 | 25 | LED matrix, 4 RGB LEDs |
| Arduino UNO R3 | 5 V | 20 | 6 | 6 (10 bit) |   | 2 |   |
| Arduino Nano | 5 V | 20 | 6 | 8 (10 bit) |   | 2 |   |
| Arduino Mega 2560 | 5 V | 70 | 15 | 16 (10 bit) |   | 6 |   |
| Arduino UNO R4 Minima | 5 V | 20 | 6 | 6 (14 bit) | 1 | 2 |   |
| Arduino UNO R4 WiFi | 5 V | 20 | 6 | 6 (14 bit) | 1 | 2 |   |
| Arduino Nano R4 | 5 V | 22 | 6 | 8 (14 bit) | 1 | 2 |   |
| ESP32 DevKit V1 | 3.3 V | 25 | 19 | 6 (12 bit) | 2 | 19 |   |
| ESP32-C3 Super Mini | 3.3 V | 13 | 13 | 5 (12 bit) |   | 13 |   |
| ESP8266 NodeMCU | 3.3 V | 11 | 8 | 1 (10 bit) |   | 8 |   |

The device types:

| Tag | Device | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DI | Button or contact | Push button, door contact, PIR, limit switch |
| AI | Analog sensor | Potentiometer, NTC, LDR, any voltage sensor |
| CNT | Pulse counter | Flow meter, energy meter, RPM |
| DO | Relay or LED | Anything that is simply on or off |
| PWM | Dimmer (PWM) | LED brightness, fan or motor speed |
| AO | Analog output | A real voltage from the DAC |
| RGB | RGB LED | On-board LED, 8 colours |
| MX | LED matrix | Text, clock, live values, graphs, icons, animations |
| VS | Virtual switch | A flag for scripts and Home Assistant |

<a id="pins-unoq-notes"></a>
### Notes on the UNO Q

- Every pin works at 3.3 V. **A0, A1 and D3 never tolerate more than 3.3 V.** A2 to A5 take at most 3.3 V when used as analog inputs.
- D3, D5, D6, D9, D10 and D11 (the six `~` pins) are the safe PWM pins. PWM on D2, D7, D8, D12, D13, SDA and SCL needs a recent UNO Q core; if a lamp does not dim there, move it to a `~` pin.
- A0 and A1 are real analog outputs (DAC). Analog inputs are 14 bit.
- The three pins CIPO, COPI and SCK of the 6-pin SPI header can be used as digital pins.
- LED1 and LED2 are driven by the Linux side, and LED2 normally shows system status. LED3 and LED4 are driven by the microcontroller.
- The 13 x 8 LED matrix has its own page: [LED matrix](#matrix).
- The bottom connector is not supported since version 2.1. Devices that sat on it are removed when an old setup is loaded, and the Log names them. Block scripts that used them are kept but switched off: in **Blocks** pick another device in their blocks, then right-click the script's first block and choose **Enable Block**.

<a id="pins-limits"></a>
### Limits of the other boards

| Board | Not offered | Keep in mind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UNO R3, Nano, Mega 2560 | - | 5 V logic. Counters only on D2 and D3 (Mega: also D18 to D21). On the Nano, A6 and A7 are analog inputs only. No internal pull-down. |
| UNO R4 Minima / WiFi | - | 5 V logic, 14-bit analog inputs, a real analog output on A0. Counters on D2 and D3. |
| Nano R4 | On-board LED, RGB LED and the Qwiic connector | 5 V logic. PWM only on the six `~` pins, counters on D2 and D3. A6 and A7 are full pins here, unlike the classic Nano. No internal pull-down. |
| ESP32 DevKit V1 | GPIO0 (BOOT button), GPIO6 to 11 (flash memory) | No pin tolerates 5 V. D34, D35, VP and VN are inputs only and have no pull resistors. Analog inputs only on D32 to D35, VP and VN. Analog output on D25 and D26 in 256 steps. At most 16 dimmers at once. D2, D5, D12 and D15 are boot pins. |
| ESP32-C3 Super Mini | GPIO11 to 17 (supply and flash), GPIO18 and 19 (USB) | Analog inputs only on IO0 to IO4, measuring up to about 2.5 V. At most 6 dimmers at once. IO2, IO8 and IO9 are boot pins; IO8 also carries the blue LED (lit when LOW), IO9 the BOOT button. |
| ESP8266 NodeMCU | GPIO6 to 11 (flash memory; also the SD2 and SD3 pads) | One analog input, A0, 0 to 3.3 V on a NodeMCU board. D0 has no pull-up, no PWM and no counter. D3, D4 and D8 are boot pins: D8 must be LOW and D3, D4 must not be held LOW while the board starts. No internal pull-down. |

> **Note:** The printed names on ESP boards are not always the GPIO numbers. QHome shows the printed name and, where it differs, the GPIO number next to it, for example D5 (GPIO14) on a NodeMCU.

<a id="pins-inputs"></a>
### Buttons and contacts

| Resistor | Wiring |
| --- | --- |
| Pull-up (contact to GND) | Contact between the pin and GND. The usual choice; no extra part needed. |
| Pull-down (contact to supply) | Contact between the pin and the board's supply: 3.3 V, or 5 V on a 5 V board. |
| None (external) | You add your own resistor, or the sensor drives the pin both ways. |

- **Low level means ON**: with a pull-up a pressed contact reads low. Leave this ticked so that pressed shows as On.
- **Debounce (ms)**: changes shorter than this are ignored. 30 ms suits buttons; use 0 for clean electronic signals.
- Where a pin has no internal resistor of the kind you picked, it becomes a plain input and you must add the resistor yourself. That is the case for pull-down on UNO R3, Nano, Mega, the R4 boards and ESP8266, and for both kinds on ESP32 D34, D35, VP, VN and NodeMCU D0.
- **Home Assistant class** only changes the icon and wording there (door, motion, smoke and so on).

<a id="pins-analog"></a>
### Analog sensors

| Show as | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Voltage (V) | reading / full scale x reference voltage |
| Percent (0-100) | reading / full scale x 100 |
| Raw ADC value | the reading itself |
| Scaled (two points) | A straight line through two points: **Input min (V)** shows **Shown at min**, **Input max (V)** shows **Shown at max**. |

- The reference voltage is 3.3 V on the UNO Q and the ESP boards, and 5 V on UNO R3, Nano, Mega, UNO R4 and Nano R4. Full scale is 1023 (10 bit), 4095 (12 bit, ESP32 and ESP32-C3) or 16383 (14 bit); see the table at the top.
- Example: a pressure sensor gives 0.5 V at 0 bar and 2.5 V at 10 bar. Choose **Scaled (two points)**, Input min 0.5, Input max 2.5, Shown at min 0, Shown at max 10, Unit bar.
- **Average over (samples)** smooths the value over the last readings (1 to 50).
- **Ignore changes below**: a new value is reported only when it differs by at least this much. 0 reports everything.
- **Report every (ms)** sets how often the board measures (50 ms to 10 minutes).

> **Warning:** Never put more on an analog pin than the board allows: 3.3 V on the UNO Q and the ESP boards (about 2.5 V is the most an ESP32-C3 measures), 5 V on the 5 V boards. Use a voltage divider for higher voltages.

<a id="pins-counter"></a>
### Pulse counters

- **Pulses per minute**: value = pulses per minute x **Multiplier**.
- **Running total**: value = all pulses so far x **Multiplier**. The total survives a restart of QHome and a reset of the board.
- Example: a flow meter gives 450 pulses per litre. With Multiplier 0.002222 (1 / 450) the rate reads in litres per minute and the total in litres.
- Which pins can count is in the **Counter** column of the table at the top. A UNO R3, Nano, UNO R4 or Nano R4 counts on 2 pins at once, a Mega or an ESP board on 6.

<a id="pins-outputs"></a>
### Outputs

- **Relay or LED**: on or off. Tick **Active-low (relay boards)** when the relay board switches on with a low level. **After a restart** decides how it starts: off, on, or as it was.
- **Dimmer (PWM)**: 0 to 100 %. **Lowest duty (%)** is the level at which the lamp or motor just starts to work; **Highest duty (%)** caps the top.
- **Analog output**: a real voltage, set in volts. On the UNO Q (A0, A1), UNO R4 and Nano R4 (A0) and ESP32 (D25, D26).
- **RGB LED**: the UNO Q's four LEDs, in eight colours: off, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white.
- **Virtual switch**: has no pin. A flag that scripts and Home Assistant can set and read.

Not supported yet: servo and tone outputs, I2C and SPI sensor drivers, CAN.

<a id="wiring"></a>
## Connecting boards

More boards extend the master: their pins behave as if they were on it. Add one in **Boards & pins > Add board**. The dialog shows the exact `config.h` lines and the wiring for your choice. Each board needs the satellite firmware once; see [Board models](#boards).

Which board can use which link:

| Board | Built in (this UNO Q) | USB cable | UART wires (D0/D1) | I2C bus | Wi-Fi (MQTT) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Arduino UNO Q | ✓ |   |   |   | ✓ |
| Arduino UNO R3 |   | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |   |
| Arduino Nano |   | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |   |
| Arduino Mega 2560 |   | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |   |
| Arduino UNO R4 Minima |   | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |   |
| Arduino UNO R4 WiFi |   | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Arduino Nano R4 |   | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |   |
| ESP32 DevKit V1 |   | ✓ | ✓ |   | ✓ |
| ESP32-C3 Super Mini |   | ✓ | ✓ |   | ✓ |
| ESP8266 NodeMCU |   | ✓ | ✓ |   | ✓ |

| Link | Wires | Boards per master |
| --- | --- | --- |
| USB cable | one USB cable | as many as there are USB ports |
| UART | TX, RX, GND | one |
| I2C | SDA, SCL, GND | several, each with its own address |
| Wi-Fi (MQTT) | none | many |

<a id="wiring-usb"></a>
### USB cable

- Plug the board into the UNO Q through a USB-C hub. The cable also powers the board, and no level shifting is needed.
- On UNO R3, Nano, Mega 2560, ESP32 DevKit and NodeMCU the USB link uses the board's serial pins, so those two pins are hatched: D0/D1, RX0/TX0 on the ESP32, RX/TX on the NodeMCU. UNO R4, Nano R4 and ESP32-C3 keep all their pins.
- **USB port**: leave it on **Automatic (first free board)** with one USB board. With several, pick the port of each so they cannot swap.
- A board that already has the satellite firmware is announced when you plug it in; see [New board found](#boards-found).

```
#define QL_LINK  QL_USB
#define QL_BAUD  115200
```

**USB helper.** Inside App Lab the Python part of an app runs in a container that may not see USB serial devices. Try without the helper first: if the board is listed under **Settings > USB boards** or announced as a new board, you do not need it. If it is not, run this on the UNO Q:

```
python3 ~/ArduinoApps/qhome/tools/qhome_usb_helper.py
```

- The helper passes every USB board on to QHome through port 7001. Such ports are listed as `helper:<name>`.
- To keep it running after a reboot, follow the comments in `tools/qhome-usb-helper.service`, or use the VS Code task **UNO Q: install the USB helper service**.
- On a PC the helper is never needed.

<a id="wiring-uart"></a>
### UART wires

- Master **D1 (TX)** to the board's RX, master **D0 (RX)** to the board's TX, GND to GND.
- Only one board per master can use this link. D0 and D1 of the master are then hatched.
- **Baud rate** (9600 to 115200) must equal `QL_BAUD` in `config.h`.
- The same wiring works through RS-485 transceivers or HC-05 / HC-12 radio modules in transparent mode.

| Board | RX pin | TX pin | Voltage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| UNO R3, Nano, Mega 2560 | D0 | D1 | 5 V: level shifter or divider on the board's TX line |
| UNO R4 Minima / WiFi, Nano R4 | D0 | D1 | 5 V: level shifter or divider on the board's TX line |
| ESP32 DevKit V1 | RX2 (GPIO16) | TX2 (GPIO17) | 3.3 V: connect directly |
| ESP32-C3 Super Mini | RX (GPIO20) | TX (GPIO21) | 3.3 V: connect directly |
| ESP8266 NodeMCU | RX (GPIO3) | TX (GPIO1) | 3.3 V: connect directly |

> **Warning:** The UNO Q's pins are 3.3 V. A 5 V board's TX line must not reach D0 directly: use a level shifter, or a divider of two resistors. The line from the master's D1 to the board's RX needs nothing.

On UNO R3, Nano, Mega 2560 and NodeMCU these pins are also the USB port's. Take the two wires off while you upload the firmware.

```
#define QL_LINK  QL_UART
#define QL_BAUD  115200
```

<a id="wiring-i2c"></a>
### I2C bus

- SDA to SDA, SCL to SCL, GND to GND, on the master's SDA / SCL header pins or its Qwiic connector. The bus needs pull-up resistors to 3.3 V.
- For UNO R3, Nano, Mega 2560, UNO R4 and Nano R4. On the satellite the bus is on A4 (SDA) and A5 (SCL); on a Mega on D20 and D21. **ESP boards cannot use this link**; use USB, UART or Wi-Fi for them.
- Several boards can share one bus. Each needs its own **I2C address** (8 to 119), the same number as `QL_I2C_ADDRESS` in its `config.h`, where it is written in hexadecimal. The dialog shows the line to copy.
- These boards are 5 V: use an I2C level shifter and keep the cables short. `QL_I2C_PULLUPS 0` keeps the board's own 5 V pull-ups off the 3.3 V bus.
- With the header bus, SDA and SCL of the master are hatched. The Qwiic connector leaves them free.

```
#define QL_LINK  QL_I2C
#define QL_I2C_ADDRESS  0x10
#define QL_I2C_PULLUPS  0
```

<a id="wiring-wifi"></a>
### Wi-Fi (MQTT)

The board joins your Wi-Fi and talks to the master's MQTT broker. For UNO R4 WiFi, ESP32, ESP32-C3, ESP8266 and other UNO Qs. The lines for `config.h`, with this master's values:

```
#define QL_LINK  QL_WIFI
#define QL_WIFI_SSID    "your-wifi"
#define QL_WIFI_PASS    "your-password"
#define QL_BOARD_ID     "kitchen"
#define QL_MASTER_HOST  "192.168.1.50"
#define QL_MASTER_PORT  1883
```

Checklist when the board stays offline:

- MQTT is on in **Settings** (built-in broker or another broker). Wi-Fi boards cannot be saved while it is off.
- The board's **Id** in QHome equals `QL_BOARD_ID`, letter for letter.
- `QL_MASTER_HOST` is an address the board can reach: the master's IP address, not `localhost`.
- If the broker has a user name and password, they are also in `QL_MQTT_USER` and `QL_MQTT_PASS`.
- ESP boards join 2.4 GHz networks only.

The link uses the topics `qlink/<board>/down`, `qlink/<board>/up` and `qlink/<board>/status`. A Wi-Fi board that reaches the broker but is not in the setup yet is announced; see [New board found](#boards-found).

<a id="wiring-offline"></a>
### When a board drops off

- Its tiles on the Dashboard turn grey and its dot turns red.
- Scripts can react with `when board ... goes offline`.
- The board keeps its outputs as they were. When it returns, the master sends its setup again.

<a id="wiring-pc"></a>
### A PC as the hub

QHome also runs on a PC without a UNO Q. USB and Wi-Fi boards work; UART and I2C links need the UNO Q's microcontroller.

```
QHOME_MODE=pc python python/main.py
```

<a id="boards"></a>
## Board models

Every board except the master runs the same satellite firmware, `satellite/qhome_satellite`. The steps are the same for all of them:

1. In **Boards & pins > Add board** choose the model and how it is connected.
2. Open `satellite/qhome_satellite` in the Arduino IDE and put the lines the dialog shows into `config.h`.
3. Choose the board under **Tools > Board** (names below) and upload once.
4. Connect the board and press **Save & apply**. Its dot turns green.

- After that nothing is uploaded again: pins are configured from this page.
- The note **This board reports that it is a ...** means the model chosen in QHome is not the board that answered. Edit the board and pick the right model.
- The master cannot upload firmware to a satellite. That always happens from a PC.
- From a terminal the same works with arduino-cli and the FQBN given in each section:

```
arduino-cli compile --upload -p <port> --fqbn <FQBN> satellite/qhome_satellite
```

> **Note:** Support for Nano R4, ESP32, ESP32-C3 and ESP8266 is new in version 2.1. The firmware was tested against a stand-in on a PC, not yet on these boards. If the Arduino IDE reports a compile error, keep the message; it points at the line to fix.

<a id="boards-unoq"></a>
### Another UNO Q (node)

1. Install QHome on the second UNO Q as usual; see [Getting started](#start-install).
2. On it, open **Settings > Role of this board** and choose **Node of another master**. Enter the master address **192.168.1.50**, MQTT port **1883** and a node name, then save. It restarts in the new role.
3. Here on the master, add a board: model **Arduino UNO Q**, connected by **Wi-Fi (MQTT)**, with the node name as its **Id**.

All pins of the node, its four LEDs and its matrix (with every matrix mode) then belong to the master. A node runs no scripts of its own. A node that reaches the broker is also announced as a new board.

<a id="boards-avr"></a>
### UNO R3, Nano, Mega 2560

- Package: **Arduino AVR Boards**, which comes with the Arduino IDE. Boards: **Arduino Uno**, **Arduino Nano**, **Arduino Mega or Mega 2560**.
- FQBN: `arduino:avr:uno`, `arduino:avr:nano`, `arduino:avr:mega`.
- Many Nano clones need **Tools > Processor > ATmega328P (Old Bootloader)** (`arduino:avr:nano:cpu=atmega328old`).
- Links: USB, UART, I2C. With USB or UART, D0 and D1 carry the link.
- 5 V logic: see [Connecting boards](#wiring-uart) before wiring them to the UNO Q's pins.

<a id="boards-r4"></a>
### UNO R4 Minima, UNO R4 WiFi, Nano R4

- Package: **Arduino UNO R4 Boards** (install it in the Boards Manager). Boards: **Arduino UNO R4 Minima**, **Arduino UNO R4 WiFi**, **Arduino Nano R4**.
- FQBN: `arduino:renesas_uno:minima`, `arduino:renesas_uno:unor4wifi`, `arduino:renesas_uno:nanor4`.
- Links: USB, UART, I2C; Wi-Fi only on the UNO R4 WiFi. The USB link does not take D0 and D1.
- 5 V logic, 14-bit analog inputs, a real analog output on A0.
- Nano R4: A6 and A7 are full pins. Its on-board LEDs and Qwiic connector are not offered.

<a id="boards-esp32"></a>
### ESP32 DevKit V1

1. In the Arduino IDE open **File > Preferences** and add this line to **Additional boards manager URLs**: `https://espressif.github.io/arduino-esp32/package_esp32_index.json`
2. In the **Boards Manager** install **esp32 by Espressif Systems**. Take version 3.x; 2.0.x works as well.
3. Choose **Tools > Board > DOIT ESP32 DEVKIT V1** (FQBN `esp32:esp32:esp32doit-devkit-v1`).
4. Fill in `config.h` and upload. If the upload stops at `Connecting....`, hold the **BOOT** button until it continues.

- Links: USB (takes RX0 and TX0), UART on **RX2 (GPIO16)** and **TX2 (GPIO17)**, Wi-Fi.
- D34, D35, VP and VN are inputs only. Analog inputs: D32, D33, D34, D35, VP, VN (12 bit). Analog outputs: D25 and D26.
- Boot pins, marked with an amber corner: D2, D5, D12, D15. **D12 must be LOW while the board starts**, so do not put a pull-up or a relay input on it.
- TX0, D5, D14 and D15 send a short burst of signals while the board starts. A relay there may click at power-up.

> **Warning:** An ESP32 works at 3.3 V. 5 V on any pin can destroy it.

<a id="boards-esp32c3"></a>
### ESP32-C3 Super Mini

1. Install the **esp32 by Espressif Systems** package as for the [ESP32](#boards-esp32).
2. Choose **Tools > Board > Nologo ESP32C3 Super Mini** (FQBN `esp32:esp32:nologo_esp32c3_super_mini`). **ESP32C3 Dev Module** works as well.
3. Set **Tools > USB CDC On Boot** to **Enabled**. The USB link needs it; without it the firmware refuses to compile.
4. Fill in `config.h` and upload. If no serial port appears, hold **BOOT**, tap **RST**, release **BOOT**.

- Links: USB (takes no pin), UART on **RX (GPIO20)** and **TX (GPIO21)**, Wi-Fi.
- Analog inputs on IO0 to IO4, up to about 2.5 V. No analog output.
- Boot pins: IO2, IO8, IO9. IO8 carries the blue LED, IO9 the BOOT button; IO9 is fine for a button to GND.
- 3.3 V only, as on every ESP board.

QHome draws the ESP32-C3 Super Mini. Other small ESP32-C3 boards have the same pins in other places; use **List view** for them.

<a id="boards-esp8266"></a>
### ESP8266 NodeMCU

1. Add this line to **Additional boards manager URLs**: `https://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json`
2. In the **Boards Manager** install **esp8266 by ESP8266 Community**.
3. Choose **Tools > Board > NodeMCU 1.0 (ESP-12E Module)** (FQBN `esp8266:esp8266:nodemcuv2`).
4. Fill in `config.h` and upload. If the PC shows no serial port, install the driver of the board's USB chip (CH340 or CP2102).

- Links: USB and UART, both on **RX (GPIO3)** and **TX (GPIO1)**, and Wi-Fi.
- The names printed on the board are not GPIO numbers: D1 is GPIO5, D2 is GPIO4, D5 is GPIO14. QHome shows both.
- One analog input, A0: 0 to 3.3 V on a NodeMCU board (a bare ESP-12 module takes only 0 to 1 V).
- D0 has no pull-up, no PWM and no counter. Boot pins: D3 (FLASH button), D4 (built-in LED, lit when LOW) and D8, which must be LOW while the board starts.
- 3.3 V only.

<a id="boards-found"></a>
### New board found

QHome notices boards that are not in the setup yet while it runs. They show as a note **New board found** at the top of **Boards & pins**, and the tab carries a count.

| What is detected | When |
| --- | --- |
| A USB board with the satellite firmware | a few seconds after it is plugged in |
| A Wi-Fi board or a UNO Q node | as soon as it connects to the master's MQTT broker |

1. Press **Add**. The dialog opens with the model and the port or id filled in.
2. Give the board a name. For a Wi-Fi board the id cannot be changed: it is the one flashed into the board.
3. Press **Save & apply**. The board goes online and its pins can get jobs. The other boards keep running; nothing restarts.

- **Ignore** hides a note in this browser.
- **Something is connected on ... but does not answer**: the port is there but no satellite firmware replied. Upload the firmware, with `QL_LINK QL_USB` and `QL_BAUD 115200`.
- **A board reports the model ...**: its firmware is newer than this QHome. Update QHome.
- Not detected: boards on UART or I2C wires, and Wi-Fi boards that do not have the master's address yet. Add those by hand with **Add board**, as before.
- To detect USB boards QHome asks every unused USB serial port once who is there. UNO R3, Nano and Mega reset when their port is opened. Start QHome with `QHOME_USB_PROBE=0` to turn this off.

<a id="blocks"></a>
## Blocks cookbook

The **Blocks** tab works like Scratch. Drag blocks from the left and snap them under a yellow "when" block. Scripts run on the master as soon as you save.

- Every "when" block starts its own script. Blocks without one on top never run.
- Scripts run side by side. `wait` and `forever` never hold up another script.
- A script that is triggered again while it runs starts over from the top.
- Devices of different boards can be mixed in one script.
- The counter under the editor shows how many scripts are running. At most 200 run at once.

| Category | Blocks |
| --- | --- |
| Events | when QHome starts; when a device turns on, turns off or changes; when a value goes above or below a limit; every N seconds, minutes or hours; at HH:MM on chosen days; when a board goes online or offline; when an MQTT message arrives |
| Devices | turn on or off, toggle, set a level, set an RGB colour; for the LED matrix: show a text, show a text for N seconds, show an icon, play an animation, show a device's value as a number or a bar, switch the view, clear |
| Sensing | is on, value of, board is online, current hour / minute / second / day of week, time is between |
| Control | wait, repeat, forever, if, if / else, wait until, repeat until, stop this script |
| Operators | arithmetic, compare, and / or / not, random, round, remainder, constrain, text, join |
| Variables | create, set, change |
| Network | publish to MQTT, the received MQTT message, write to the log |

<a id="blocks-time"></a>
### Time blocks

- `at 07:30 on weekdays` starts a script at that minute. Days: every day, weekdays, the weekend, or one day of the week.
- `time is between 22:00 and 06:00` also works across midnight.
- `current hour`, `minute`, `second` and `day of week (1 = Monday)` give numbers for comparisons.
- `every 10 minutes` repeats from the moment the setup was saved, not on the clock.
- All of them use the time zone chosen in **Settings**. In a zone with daylight saving, a script set to a time that occurs twice in the night the clocks go back runs once, and a script set to a time that does not exist in the night the clocks go forward (02:00 to 02:59 in most of Europe) runs as soon as the clock jumps. See [Troubleshooting](#faq-timezone).

<a id="blocks-recipes"></a>
### Recipes

The names in square brackets are your own devices and the choices of the dropdowns.

**1. A button toggles a light on another board**

1. `when [Door button] turns [on]`
2. `toggle [Garage light]`

The button may be on the UNO Q and the light on a board in the garage.

**2. A fan follows the temperature**

1. `when [Temperature] goes [above] 28`, then `turn [Fan] [on]`
2. A second script: `when [Temperature] goes [below] 26`, then `turn [Fan] [off]`

"Goes above" fires once, at the moment the limit is crossed. Two different limits keep the fan from switching on and off around a single value.

**3. A night light on motion**

1. `when [Motion] turns [on]`
2. `if <time is between 22:00 and 06:00> then`
3. inside it: `turn [Hall light] [on]`, `wait 120 seconds`, `turn [Hall light] [off]`

New motion starts the script over, so the light stays on as long as someone moves.

**4. Good morning on the matrix**

1. `at 07:30 on [weekdays]`
2. `show icon [sun] on [Matrix]`, `wait 5 seconds`
3. `show [Temperature] on [Matrix] as [a number]`, `wait 60 seconds`
4. `switch [Matrix] to [As set up]`

The last block hands the matrix back to what its setup says. See [LED matrix](#matrix-override).

**5. An alarm when a board goes offline**

1. `when board [Garage] goes [offline]`
2. `set [LED 3] colour to [red]`
3. `publish [garage offline] to MQTT topic [home/alerts]`
4. `write [Garage board is offline] to the log`

<a id="blocks-variables"></a>
### Variables

- Variables show on the Dashboard under **Script variables**.
- They keep their values through **Save & apply**, but start at 0 again when QHome restarts. Use a **Virtual switch** for a state that must survive a restart.

<a id="matrix"></a>
## LED matrix

The UNO Q has 13 x 8 LEDs with 8 brightness levels. The picture is built on the master, so the matrix of a UNO Q node can do everything described here as well.

Give the matrix a job in **Boards & pins** (click it on the drawing), then choose under **Show** what it displays.

<a id="matrix-modes"></a>
### The nine modes

| Show | What you see | Settings | Name in commands |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Text | The text, centred when it fits and scrolling when it does not. | Text, Scroll speed | `text` |
| Clock | Hours and minutes in the time zone from Settings: bright hours, dim minutes, two blinking dots. | 12-hour clock | `clock` |
| Live value | The value of one device, with its unit when that fits. | Device to show | `value` |
| Bar or graph | A level bar, or a graph of the last readings, of a device with a number value. | Device to show, Draw as, Value at empty, Value at full, Graph: seconds per column | `bar` |
| Animation | One of six animations. | Animation, Speed | `anim` |
| Icon | One of fourteen icons. | Icon | `icon` |
| Board status | Boards online and in total, for example 3/4; one dot in the bottom row per board; a dot at the top right for MQTT. | - | `status` |
| Web address | Scrolls the address of this page, for example 192.168.1.50:7000. Shows NO NETWORK when there is none. | Scroll speed | `ip` |
| Off | Dark. | - | `off` |

- **Brightness (1-7)** applies to every mode.
- **Text**: the matrix shows capital letters only. Turkish letters appear without their marks (Ş as S, Ğ as G). Signs it knows: `. , : ! ' - + = / % ? < > ( ) °`. Any other sign shows as `?`.
- Write `{id}` in a text to insert the live value of the device with that id, for example `TEMP {temp}`.
- **Scroll speed (ms per column)**: 40 is fast, 1000 very slow; 120 is the default.
- **Live value** drops the space, then the unit, when the text is wider than the matrix: `5 V`, `23C`, `23.5`. A longer value scrolls.
- **Level bar**: empty at **Value at empty**, full at **Value at full**. With both the same it runs from 0 to 100.
- **History graph**: 13 columns, the newest on the right. **Graph: seconds per column** sets the time span: 5 seconds give about one minute, 300 give about one hour. With both values the same, the graph scales itself to what is on screen.

<a id="matrix-icons"></a>
### Icons

| Icon | Name in commands |
| --- | --- |
| smile | `smile` |
| sad face | `sad` |
| heart | `heart` |
| check mark | `check` |
| cross | `cross` |
| Wi-Fi | `wifi` |
| house | `house` |
| sun | `sun` |
| moon | `moon` |
| bell | `bell` |
| warning | `warn` |
| lock | `lock` |
| arrow up | `up` |
| arrow down | `down` |

<a id="matrix-anims"></a>
### Animations

| Animation | Name in commands |
| --- | --- |
| heartbeat | `heartbeat` |
| wave | `wave` |
| rain | `rain` |
| sparkle | `sparkle` |
| spinner | `spinner` |
| bouncing dot | `bounce` |

**Speed (1-9)** sets how fast an animation runs.

<a id="matrix-override"></a>
### Who decides what is shown

Three things can set the picture. The first one in this list that exists wins:

1. A **timed show**: "show this for N seconds". When the time is up the previous view returns.
2. A **change** made by a script, by the Dashboard or over MQTT. It stays until the next change or until **As set up** is chosen.
3. The **setup**: what **Show** says in Boards & pins.

- On the Dashboard the matrix tile has a dropdown with **As set up** and the nine modes. A choice there applies at once, without saving. While a change is active the tile shows **Changed here**, with the seconds left for a timed show.
- Changes are forgotten when QHome restarts; the matrix then shows its setup.
- Saving a setup in which the matrix's own settings changed also clears them. Saving anything else leaves them alone.

<a id="matrix-blocks"></a>
### Blocks for the matrix

| Block | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `show [text] on [Matrix]` | Shows the text until something else is shown. |
| `show [text] on [Matrix] for [5] seconds` | A timed show. The script waits that long, then the previous view returns. |
| `show icon [heart] on [Matrix]` | Shows an icon. |
| `play animation [rain] on [Matrix]` | Plays an animation. |
| `show [Temperature] on [Matrix] as [a number]` | Shows a device's live value, as a number or as a bar. |
| `switch [Matrix] to [Clock]` | Switches to As set up, Clock, Board status, Web address or Off. |
| `clear [Matrix]` | Dark until something else is shown. |

<a id="matrix-commands"></a>
### MQTT and commands

| Topic | Direction | Payload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `qhome/<id>/set` | in | a text to show |
| `qhome/<id>/mode/set` | in | one of the strings below |
| `qhome/<id>/mode` | out, retained | the mode drawn now: one of the nine names |
| `qhome/<id>/state` | out, retained | the text or value shown; a fixed word such as `[clock]` for modes that move |

| Send to mode/set | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `auto` | back to the setup |
| `clock`, `status`, `ip`, `off` | that mode |
| `icon:heart` | the icon with that name |
| `anim:rain` | the animation with that name |
| `value:temp` | the live value of the device `temp` |
| `bar:temp` | the bar or graph of the device `temp` |
| `text:HELLO` | that text |

In Home Assistant the matrix appears as a text entity and a select entity named "&lt;name> mode". Over HTTP the same commands go to `/api/cmd`; this one shows a text for five seconds:

```
curl -X POST http://192.168.1.50:7000/api/cmd -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"id": "matrix", "action": "text", "value": {"text": "HI {temp}", "secs": 5}}'
```

<a id="mqtt"></a>
## MQTT and Home Assistant

QHome speaks MQTT so that Home Assistant and other programs can see and switch your devices. Choose the mode under **Settings > MQTT and Home Assistant**:

| Mode | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Built-in broker | QHome is the broker itself, on port 1883. Nothing else to install. |
| Use another broker | QHome connects to a broker you already have, for example Mosquitto. |
| Off | No MQTT. Boards connected by Wi-Fi cannot be used. |

<a id="mqtt-ha"></a>
### Home Assistant

1. In Home Assistant open **Settings > Devices & services > Add integration** and choose **MQTT**.
2. Broker: **192.168.1.50**, port: **1883**, and the user name and password if you set them in QHome.
3. The devices appear on their own, together with one "online" sensor per board.

- **Home Assistant auto-discovery** must be ticked. **Discovery prefix** stays `homeassistant` unless you changed it in Home Assistant.
- When Home Assistant restarts, QHome sends the device list again.
- A device you remove in QHome disappears from Home Assistant too.

| Device in QHome | Entity in Home Assistant |
| --- | --- |
| Button or contact | binary_sensor |
| Analog sensor, Pulse counter | sensor |
| Relay or LED, Virtual switch | switch; a relay can be shown as light instead (**Show in Home Assistant as**) |
| Dimmer (PWM) | light with brightness |
| Analog output | number, in volts |
| RGB LED | select with the eight colours |
| LED matrix | text, and a select for the mode |

**Home Assistant class** on a sensor or contact only changes its icon and unit handling there.

<a id="mqtt-topics"></a>
### Topics

Every topic starts with the node name from Settings, here **qhome**. `<id>` is the id of a device.

| Topic | Direction | Payload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `qhome/<id>/state` | out, retained | `ON` or `OFF`, a number, a colour name or a text |
| `qhome/<id>/set` | in | `ON`, `OFF`, `TOGGLE`, a number, a colour name or a text |
| `qhome/<id>/level` | out, retained | dimmer level, 0 to 100 |
| `qhome/<id>/level/set` | in | dimmer level, 0 to 100 |
| `qhome/<matrix>/mode` | out, retained | what the LED matrix shows now |
| `qhome/<matrix>/mode/set` | in | `clock`, `icon:heart`, `auto` and so on; see [LED matrix](#matrix-commands) |
| `qhome/status` | out, retained | `online` while QHome is connected |
| `qhome/board/<board>/state` | out, retained | `ON` when that board is online, else `OFF` |

Topics that start with `qlink/` carry the link to Wi-Fi boards. Leave them alone.

<a id="mqtt-scripts"></a>
### MQTT in scripts

- `publish [text] to MQTT topic [topic]` sends any message.
- `when an MQTT message arrives on [topic]` starts a script. The topic may contain the wildcards `+` (one level) and `#` (everything below).
- `MQTT message` is the text that arrived.

<a id="mqtt-security"></a>
### Security

- Set a broker **User name** and **Password**. Without them anyone on your network can switch your outputs.
- The web page uses plain HTTP. A web password is sent with every request without encryption, so keep QHome on your own network.
- To reach it through a web server you already run, forward to port 7000:

```
server {
    listen 80;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:7000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
    }
}
```

<a id="faq"></a>
## Troubleshooting

<a id="faq-address"></a>
### Where is the page? What is the address?

- App Lab opens the page when the app starts, unless a web password is set.
- The **Python console** of App Lab and the **Log** tab show a framed block with `http://<address>:7000` after every start, and again when the address changes.
- The **Serial Monitor** of App Lab shows `=== QHome ===` and the address every 30 seconds, so wait up to half a minute after opening it. Once it has appeared, press any key there to see it again at once. `QHome: waiting for the Linux side...` means the Python part has not started yet.
- An LED matrix whose **Show** is **Web address** scrolls it.
- The **System** panel on the Dashboard lists every address under **Network**.
- `http://<board-name>.local:7000` works on most networks.
- Nothing answers: the app must be running in App Lab, and your device must be on the same network as the board.

<a id="faq-password"></a>
### The web password

- With a web password the browser asks for a user name and a password. Any user name works.
- App Lab cannot open a page that asks for a password. Open the address yourself.
- Forgot it: on the board, open `data/config.json` in the app's folder, set `"web_password"` under `"device"` to `""`, and restart the app in App Lab.
- The password travels unencrypted (plain HTTP). It keeps housemates out, not attackers.

<a id="faq-timezone"></a>
### The time is wrong

- Choose the zone under **Settings > Time zone**: first the **Region**, then the **City or offset**. **Use this browser's zone** fills both in.
- **Time on the board now** under the picker shows the clock that scripts and the matrix use. The System panel on the Dashboard shows it too.
- A named zone such as Europe/Berlin follows daylight saving by itself. A fixed offset such as UTC+3 never changes.
- The board has no clock battery; it sets its clock from the internet. If QHome warns that the board's clock is minutes off, check the board's network connection.
- On a PC without a time zone database (Windows) named zones run with a fixed offset and without daylight saving; QHome says so in Settings.
- A setup from an older version, with an offset in hours, is converted to a fixed offset such as UTC+3 when it is loaded.

<a id="faq-mcu"></a>
### "The microcontroller does not answer yet"

This line in the Log means the Linux side cannot reach the sketch on the UNO Q's microcontroller. QHome keeps trying. Check in App Lab that **Arduino_RouterBridge** is added under Sketch Libraries, then press **Run** again so that the sketch is compiled and uploaded.

<a id="faq-offline"></a>
### A board's dot stays red

The text next to the board's name in **Boards & pins** says what its link is waiting for.

| Link | Check |
| --- | --- |
| USB | Is the board listed under **Settings > USB boards**? If not, start the USB helper. Is the right port chosen? Does `QL_LINK` say `QL_USB`? |
| UART | TX to RX and RX to TX (crossed)? GND connected? The same baud rate on both sides? The right pins on the board (ESP32: RX2 and TX2)? |
| I2C | The same address in QHome and in `config.h`? Pull-ups to 3.3 V? A level shifter for a 5 V board? Short cables? |
| Wi-Fi | Wi-Fi name and password right? A 2.4 GHz network? The master's address in `QL_MASTER_HOST`? MQTT on? The id equal to `QL_BOARD_ID`? |

- **This board reports that it is a ...**: the model chosen in QHome is not the board that answered.
- An ESP board that does not start, or restarts over and over, with your wiring attached: something holds a boot pin (amber corner) at the wrong level. Move that wire to another pin.

<a id="faq-save"></a>
### "Not saved. Fix these first"

QHome checks a setup before it applies it and lists what is wrong. The list is in English. Common entries:

| Message | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Pin ... is used by both ... and ... | Two devices sit on one pin. |
| ... is used by a board link and is not free | The pin carries a link (hatched). |
| ... cannot do that | The pin lacks that ability, for example PWM. |
| Wi-Fi boards need MQTT | Turn MQTT on in Settings. |
| Only one board can use the UART on D0/D1 | Use USB, I2C or Wi-Fi for the others. |
| ... pick the device whose value the matrix shows | A matrix in Live value or Bar mode, or a matrix block, has no device chosen. |
| Time zone ... is not known | Pick a zone from the list in Settings. |

<a id="faq-pins"></a>
### Pins and values

- **A pin is hatched**: a board link uses it. Change the link or use another pin.
- **A dimmer does not dim** on UNO Q pins D2, D7, D8, D12, D13, SDA or SCL: PWM there needs a recent UNO Q core. Use D3, D5, D6, D9, D10 or D11.
- **An analog value jumps**: raise **Average over (samples)**, set **Ignore changes below**, and check that the voltage stays within the pin's range.
- **A button reads the wrong way round**: change **Low level means ON**.
- **A relay clicks when the board starts**: on ESP boards some pins send signals during start-up; their notes say so. Use another pin.
- **Devices are gone after an update**: version 2.1 removed the UNO Q's bottom connector. The Log lists the removed devices; put them on header pins. Scripts that used them are switched off (hatched in **Blocks**): pick the new device in their blocks, then right-click the first block and choose **Enable Block**.

<a id="faq-scripts"></a>
### Scripts

- **A script does not run**: it needs a yellow "when" block on top. The counter under the editor shows how many scripts are running. The Log reports `A script stopped with an error`.
- **A timed script fires at the wrong hour**: see [The time is wrong](#faq-timezone).
- **Scripts stopped**: they run on the master. While it is off or restarting nothing runs.

<a id="faq-ha"></a>
### Devices are missing in Home Assistant

- Is MQTT on, and **Home Assistant auto-discovery** ticked?
- Is the **Discovery prefix** the one Home Assistant uses (normally `homeassistant`)?
- Do Home Assistant and QHome use the same broker, with the same user name and password?
- The **MQTT** line next to the navigation shows whether QHome is connected to the broker.

<a id="faq-backup"></a>
### Back up or move a setup

**Settings > Backup > Download setup (.json)** saves everything: boards, devices, scripts and settings. **Load a setup file** reads it back; press **Save & apply** afterwards. Files from older versions are converted when they are loaded.
